"I should like to congratulate our lads on their excellent wins in the I.O.W. and Kent races (held the same day) and particularly Barry Sawyer who has produced a string of consistently good performances.

Lacey: Belgrave's most improved runner BARRY SAWYER seen here during the Hogs Back '9½' in which he finished 14th. In last year's Club '7' he was 20th (!) 6½ minutes behind the winner - this year he won by over a minute!!
Barry Sawyer moved through the field after a mile and had little difficulty in gaining third place, while Dick Shackleford - always to the fore - finished fourth.
STAGE 4 - Barry Sawyer (26:15. 8th) This stage had been given to one of our most improved runners who was performing in a "Brighton" for the first time.
Let this in no way, however, detract from Alan Black's performance as he had the rapidly improving Barry Sawyer to beat as well as such old hands as Newell, MaClean, and Davies.

Barry Sawyer will remember this day for many a long year - he will never be allowed to forget it! Taking time out of a race, however short, usually precludes any chance of winning, and Barry's short sojourn into the bushes of Knowle Park meant the loss of some 150 places which even to a fit man like…
Barry Sawyer endeavour[illegible] to take over and at halfway was lying 4th but he too gave way in the end to finish 6th with a fast-finishing Linstead close behind.
(I understand that at this stage a man named Penney was causing some comment by being in a forward position in the field) At the end of the first lap Barry Sawyer had opened up a useful lead with C.
Cheers to Ron Linstead, Barry Sawyer, and the terrible twins Joe D. and D. Jones who have shown good form this year, also to Brian Johnston who had an excellent run in his first '10' at Walton.
The most improved Belgravian of the year, Barry Sawyer, also started in one of the leading groups, whilst Ron Linstead was once more holding back.
At the half-way mark, with the long uphill drag over, Barry Sawyer was still in contact with the leaders and Clive Shippen was making steady progress through the field with a group in the forties.
Our three 'A' team runners in this event Barry Sawyer, Chas. Walker and Bill Kerr had a most successful afternoon's competition.
At the end of the first lap Barry Sawyer had a slight lead over Davies, Linstead, Walker & Kerr; the latter giving the impression of only coasting.

Bill Kerr and Barry Sawyer have been most unfortunate with injuries and we did not have them both fully fit for any race. Ken Miller has been completely out of training with severe back trouble, Alan Black with a fractured foot, and Charlie Dabbs is still travelling the long road back to fitness.

On paper we had the strongest team of the day but through injury Barry Sawyer was forced to withdraw and for various reasons best known only to themselves others who had been carded failed to appear and we could start only 9 runners which precluded us from winning the Cup for the lowest score for a full team of twelve.

Our Captain Clive Shippen gained places over the last lap to be our second man home, passing Barry Sawyer, still suffering from the injury which had kept him out of the South of Thames race three weeks earlier.
A below-form Barry Sawyer ran Stage 4 for us, and lost considerable ground on the teams ahead, but his recent injury came thro' this test satisfactorily and this was a welcome consolation.

Ron Linstead and Barry Sawyer started steadily and moved through the field well, Ron in particular was well into his stride. Eric Gebbett who has been steadily approaching his old form was our 5th man home in 219th place, but we had to go back to a courageous Joe Dooley (426) for our 6th scorer, it…

The seventh and eighth legs were taken by reserves, and although both John Moore and David Jones flogged themselves to the utmost, they were not really fit enough for this type of competition, and we had to drop back to ninth some 6 mins. behind Portsmouth when Barry Sawyer took over.
The 4th movement of this Belgrave composition was played by Barry Sawyer who at last seemed to be rid of the numerous injuries which had recently been chasing themselves up and down each of his legs.
STAGE V - Barry Sawyer (22:28 17th fastest) Barry who for weeks has been troubled with strained muscles was not at his best and before the end of the Redhill stage was again limping badly.

"Fresh" from his South African exploits over 53 miles of hard undulating road, Ron Linstead showed that a mere 6 on a level track at Battersea was really quite a cake-walk by beating Pat Newell and Barry Sawyer by 120 yards and 180 yards respectively and so now holds the 'Tom Carter Cup' for this event.

John Moore had a steady run and Ron Linstead and Barry Sawyer consolidated our position amongst the leading four. Gerry North then took over for the penultimate stage and showed everyone what a great road-runner he is by smashing Hogan's course record by 9 seconds, to record a fantastic 12:38.

Barry Sawyer took over in 5th place and he quickly passed his S.L.H. rival and whilst running steadily did not quite manage to produce the same spark that he had shown in recent weeks although it must be conceded that he was very much on his own and so was not hard pressed.
CENTRE RIGHT: Barry Sawyer hands over to Gerry North at the end of stage 8. LOWER CENTRE: Gerry storms past a Belgrave Supporters coach during his devastating run on stage 9.

Cambridge Road as usual, sorted the sheep from the goats and Barry Sawyer returning once more to the form he showed about a year ago, pulled away from Eric Gebbett and Jack Brown who were renewing the battle they enjoyed in the Poly Relay only a week before.

In the absence of Barry Sawyer, Ken Miller, Clive Shippen, Laurie O'Hara, Derek Crookes and George Williams from the A team our hopes of a place as in the 1961 race were reduced to nil and the best we could do was to take 12th position out of the 69 teams that finished.

Jack Brown had to make full use of his experience to pull back Tony Fairclough and John Davies in the later stages but eventually he got away from them and was fast catching Barry Sawyer in the run in.

However, he and Barry Sawyer (foot injury) were plucky starters in our depleted team. We still had fair hopes at the start but the course disposed of them as well and Belgrave were written off in 8th place, for Sawyer had to retire and Bill Kerr's shoe was split by the ice, forcing him to withdraw as well.
In the Insurance A.A. 5 miles cross-country championship, held on December 8th, Barry Sawyer finished 2nd to Woodford's Tony Lewis.

Barry Sawyer came home on Stage 4 with an 8 second lead from Portsmouth(Salvat) and it seemed that our opponents would go on for ever changing places behind us while Belgrave, unostentatiously, held the van.

On this stage, Barry Sawyer running for the 'B' team produced one of his best ever relay runs to take eighth place in a very good time. Away went the indomitable Charlie Walker on the 2nd stage in pursuit of the Valley and in great form, he soon caught Hawkes and turned our four secs. deficit into a similar lead.
Barry Sawyer, after his excellent showing in the T.V.H. Relay was selected for the 2nd stage, but it was obvious that Barry was not at his best.

Blackpool's promising junior Tony Byrne brought his team home in first place on Stage 1 with Barry Sawyer 8th, 49 seconds down. On a wet and windy evening, and on a soft track, Barry Sawyer romped to a deserved win over Laurie O'Hara and Charlie Walker to take this Club Championship and the "Griffin Cup" for the first time.
BOTTOM RIGHT:Barry Sawyer finishes 9th in the Poly marathon with 2:28:08 and becomes Belgrave's marathon champion and record holder.
Barry Sawyer represented Hampshire in the Inter-County '20' at Victoria Park on June 1st, and was their first man home, finishing 16th in 1:52:57.

From left to right, Norman Stairs, Barry Sawyer, Alan Bishop, Len Bishop, John Moore, Charlie Walker, Denis Jones, and Derek Crookes. This picture was taken at Windsor Castle just before they were sent on their way by Her Majesty The Queen.
At 5 miles (26:30) a group of ten had broken clear and included our own Barry Sawyer and Chas. Walker - both battling also for the 'Lady Fell' Shield and Club Championship.
Barry Sawyer was 8th in the Hadleigh '6' on August 10th with a time of 31:18. Mel Batty was the winner in a record 29:58.

Gerry North has given many of the boys the right kind of leadership and now in his brother Geoff, Barry Sawyer, Tony Fairclough, John Thresher, Dave Cocks and others we have athletes of international potential.
Following the presentation of a Senior Honours Badge to Barry Sawyer for his excellent run in the Poly Marathon, the election of officers took place.

Barry Sawyer who is being developed into a first leg specialist brought us into third place on the initial stage, only three seconds behind the leader who was none other than Charlie Walker running for our 'B' team!
To provide a little variety Barry Sawyer, who started in the previous two relays, was moved to Stage 2 and Charlie Dabbs was given first crack of the whip.

Barry Sawyer was our first runner and we had every hope of a good start for Barry had been showing great form during the preceding weeks. Our confidence was well proved for in a very relaxed and easy manner he trailed the leaders over the first three miles and then left them to race ahead up Cedars…

With a view to possible "Brighton" placings, Barry Sawyer was tried again on first leg---a move which produced a winning lead right away. Barry just shot away from the pack with 1½ miles to go and handed over to Charlie Dabbs with a 26 seconds lead.

Another episode in the annals of Belgrave Harriers was recorded at Stompond Lane track, Walton, on October 19th---writes Gordon Doubleday--- when Barry Sawyer, at the peak of form, set a new World's best mark for 25 miles of 2:17:10.

After cheering Barry Sawyer on to a Worlds Best Performance 25 miles track run during the morning, Gerry North had sufficient energy left in the afternoon to pulverise a record field of 151 in the 10 miles road race.
Of our other runners Barry Sawyer, Charlie Dabbs and John Thresher performed well and John Moore was also prominent in a very strong field. A Club handicap was held in conjunction and D.C.

By the time this issue of the "Belgravian" appears, Barry Sawyer, our marathon champion and record holder will almost certainly be in South Africa preparing for the 54 mile Durban - Pietermaritzburg Comrades marathon to be run on 30th May.

Barry Sawyer finished fresher than anyone---mainly due to inadequate footwear----and Laurie O'Hara ran a very sound race at 132. Geoff.North (137) did not make the first 100 as expected but did quite well on a limited training period.
Barrie Sawyer regained the lead on the 3rd leg with a good run and this was maintained by Jack Brown, Trevor Hart and Arthur Bruce on legs 4, 5, and 6.

Alan Black who had come in as reserve to take the place of Barrie Sawyer, who was suffering from a bad cold, ran well to take us up to 2nd place, about 10 secs. ahead of Walton, but Portsmouth through Martin Hyman, opened up a big lead on this leg of 4½ miles.

STAGE I - Barry Sawyer (21:17 - 18th fastest) In the light of his good running at Ilford and his first class performance last October, Barry was allocated the first stage, although he had been forced to miss the road championship through illness and his full recovery was in doubt.

Barry Sawyer had a poor start, never got going, and although finishing in the twenties was nearly a minute behind Pat. Perhaps this was the moment he should have stepped down in favour of Pat Newell for the big event but 5 days away.

Barry Sawyer,now established in South Africa is recovering from the achilles tendon trouble which put him out of the Comrades Marathon. He has worked up to 75 miles per week so far and is enthusiastic about his running, "training here has everything- scenic roads(hilly),sandy beaches,giant dunes, go…
Barry Sawyer still seems to be getting in plenty of running in South-Africa. He is now living in Cape Town where he will remain until he moves to New Zealand in November.

Barry Sawyer won the Victorian "King of the Mountains" 20 mile race in Australia and now has his name inscribed alongside that of past winner Percy Cerutty.

BARRY SAWYER is still very close to that king of the coaches, Percy Cerutty. Barry found himself quite shocked recently when he found the 72 yrs old Cerutty looking tired after a weightlifting exhibition at a sports store.

Congratulations to BARRY SAWYER on the birth of his Australian daughter. The joy of the occasion helped to temper the disappointment he suffered in December when gastro-enteritis broke his remarkable training sequence of 708 consecutive days.

No one can cover an airmail letter-form so adeptly as BARRY SAWYER. '26 miles to Home' Barry Sawyer - Aussie based Barry has come up with another sure-fire hit which will keep the home based boys struggling to keep pace.

Yet another immaculate letter has been received from BARRY SAWYER in distant Australia (South Yarra, Melbourne). Barry, who is the Victorian State marathon champion has fought his way to personal bests from 1500 metres to the marathon, despite worsening achilles tendon trouble.

Belgrave's former marathon champion and record holder BARRY SAWYER (he lost his record this year to the man he calls "the late Trevor Hart") continues to write regularly from Australia and sends his regards and defiance to all at Belgrave Hall.

Knocking 2 mins-10secs off the time set by Barry Sawyer in 1963. Clive, not to be outdone by 'T.K', improved his own performance of 1969 by just on 12½ minutes to take a well deserved 2nd place in the Club Championship.
Barry Sawyer requests Training Schedule from Trevor Hart.

From Sydney to Melbourne, where BARRY SAWYER has resumed training again after several months of complete inactivity due to the severe achilles tendon troubles he has been experiencing these last two years.

Trevor Hart first captured the Belgrave Harriers' marathon record when he clocked 2hrs. 25m. 58s. in last year's Polytechnic race from Windsor to Chiswick - lowering Barry Sawyer's 1963 time of 2hrs. 28m. 08s.
